etymology: From “sovereign” (Latin superanus, supreme) and “grace” (Latin gratia, favour); the Reformed confession that saving grace is bestowed freely and effectually according to God's sovereign will alone.
biblical_def: Sovereign grace is the Reformed and biblical confession that the saving favour of God is bestowed freely, unconditionally, and effectually according to His own sovereign purpose, and not according to anything foreseen or done in the creature. It is grace that not only offers but accomplishes, not only invites but raises the dead. The apostle declares it root and branch: salvation is by grace through faith, and that not of ourselves, it is the gift of God; it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy; God saved us and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace given us in Christ before the world began. The doctrine gathers up the whole of the Reformed soteriology: unconditional election, particular redemption, the effectual call, and the perseverance of the saints are all expressions of one truth, that God is the author and finisher of salvation from first to last. The dictionary holds sovereign grace against every form of synergism, which makes the decisive difference in salvation lie in the sinner's will rather than in God's mercy. Grace is sovereign because the fallen will cannot and will not turn to God of itself; the same grace that ordains the end provides and applies the means, quickening the dead, granting faith and repentance as gifts, and keeping His own to the end. The proper fruit of the doctrine is not licence but humility, gratitude, and worship, for the saved sinner owes everything and can boast in nothing but the Lord.
webster_summary: The Reformed confession that saving grace is bestowed freely, unconditionally, and effectually according to God's sovereign purpose alone, not according to anything in the creature; the monergism that quickens the dead and keeps His own to the end.
webster_full: SOVEREIGN GRACE, noun phrase. The free, unconditional, and effectual saving favour of God, bestowed according to His sovereign will.
Salvation is by grace, and that not of ourselves; it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8).
It is not of him that willeth nor that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Romans 9:16).
It gathers up election, particular redemption, effectual calling, and perseverance.
Its fruit is humility and worship, for the saved sinner can boast in nothing but the Lord.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
corruption_summary: Synergism makes the decisive difference in salvation lie in the sinner's free will rather than in God's mercy, and the antinomian abuses sovereign grace as a licence to sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption of sovereign grace is synergism—the Arminian, semi-Pelagian, and Pelagian schemes that make the will of the creature the deciding factor in salvation, so that grace merely assists a power the sinner already has, or waits upon a choice he must first make. The dictionary names this as a departure from Scripture, which teaches that the natural man is dead in trespasses, cannot receive the things of the Spirit, and is turned only by a grace that quickens the dead. To shift the decisive cause from God's mercy to man's will is to make man, not God, the author of the difference between the saved and the lost, and so to rob grace of its name (Romans 11:6).

The opposite corruption is the antinomian abuse that hears “sovereign grace” as a licence to sin, reasoning that since salvation is wholly of God, holiness does not matter. The apostle anticipated and crushed this: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Romans 6:1-2). The same sovereign grace that justifies also sanctifies; it does not leave its objects in their sins but conforms them to Christ. The dictionary holds the balance: grace is free and unconditional in its bestowal, and unfailingly fruitful in its effect, producing the humility, gratitude, and holiness that mark the truly saved.
roots_summary: From the Latin gratia (favour, that which is freely given) and the idea of God's supreme rule; the Greek charis (grace) and eleeo (to show mercy) ground the doctrine.
roots_lines: Charis, Greek, grace, free unmerited favour.
Eleeo, Greek, to show mercy, “of God that sheweth mercy” (Romans 9:16).
Monos + ergon, the root of “monergism,” God working alone in regeneration.
Prothesis, Greek, purpose, God's eternal design behind the call (2 Timothy 1:9).
The sovereignty of God grounds the freeness: He has mercy on whom He will.
usage: The pastor preached sovereign grace to humble the proud and comfort the despairing, for salvation is God's work from first to last.
He answered the synergist that grace which only assists a willing sinner could never raise a dead one.
She rejoiced that the same grace which chose her before the world also kept her, and would bring her home.

etymology: From the Latin gratia (favour, kindness, thanks), rendering the Greek charis and the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (lovingkindness); the unmerited favour of God toward sinners.
biblical_def: Grace is the free and unmerited favour of God toward sinners, the disposition of His heart by which He blesses the undeserving and saves the lost wholly apart from their works. The word translates the Greek charis and answers to the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (covenant lovingkindness). Its essence is that it is unearned: where sin abounded, grace did much more abound; and if salvation be by grace, then it is no more of works, otherwise grace is no more grace. The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared, teaching as well as saving, for grace is not bare pardon but a transforming power. Of Christ's fulness His people receive grace for grace. The Reformed tradition distinguishes uses of the word: common grace, the undeserved kindness by which God restrains evil, sustains the world, and gives rain and fruitful seasons to the just and unjust alike; and saving (special) grace, the effectual favour by which He regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies His elect. The dictionary holds grace against two perennial errors. Legalism would mix works with grace, making the favour of God a wage owed to merit; but grace and merit cannot be compounded without destroying grace. Antinomianism would divorce grace from holiness, making it a cloak for sin; but the same grace that saves also teaches the saved to deny ungodliness. True grace is free in its giving and fruitful in its working, the fountain of the whole Christian life from the new birth to glory.
webster_summary: The free, unmerited favour of God toward sinners (Greek charis); distinguished into common grace toward all and saving grace toward the elect; free in its giving, fruitful in its working, opposed alike to legalism and antinomianism.
webster_full: GRACE, noun. [Latin gratia; Greek charis.] The free and unmerited favour of God toward sinners.
Its essence is that it is unearned: by grace, and not of works (Romans 11:6).
Common grace restrains evil and sustains the world for just and unjust alike.
Saving grace regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies the elect.
It is free in giving and fruitful in working, teaching the saved to deny ungodliness (Titus 2:11-12).
scriptures: And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more work.
Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound:
Tit 2:11
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
Joh 1:16
And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.
corruption_summary: Legalism compounds works with grace until grace is no longer grace; antinomianism divorces grace from holiness and makes it a cloak for sin. The modern “cheap grace” flattens it into mere tolerance.
corruption_paragraphs: Legalism, the perennial corruption of grace, mingles works with God's favour, treating salvation as partly earned, so that the sinner contributes his merit and grace fills up the remainder. The apostle declares this impossible: if it be of works, it is no more grace. Rome's system of merit, penance, and the treasury of the saints is the most developed form, but the legalist heart appears wherever a man hopes to commend himself to God by his doing. The dictionary recovers grace as wholly free, lest the cross be made void.

The opposite corruption is antinomian and, in its modern dress, sentimental. “Cheap grace,” in Bonhoeffer's phrase, preaches forgiveness without repentance and acceptance without transformation, until grace becomes a synonym for tolerance and a permission to sin. But the grace of God that brings salvation also teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts. The dictionary holds the two truths the apostle never separated: grace is received by faith alone, apart from all works; and the grace that justifies invariably sanctifies, for it is the power of God unto a holy life and not merely a verdict that leaves the sinner unchanged.
roots_summary: From the Latin gratia and the Greek charis (favour freely given), with the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (covenant lovingkindness) behind the Old Testament idea.
roots_lines: Charis, Greek, grace, favour freely and undeservedly given.
Chen, Hebrew, favour or graciousness, as “Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”
Chesed, Hebrew, steadfast covenant love or lovingkindness.
Gratia, Latin, favour, kindness, also thanks, the root of the English word.
“Grace for grace” (John 1:16) names the inexhaustible supply from Christ's fulness.
usage: The preacher distinguished common grace, which sends rain on the just and unjust, from the saving grace that regenerates the elect.
He warned against cheap grace, which preaches pardon without repentance and acceptance without holiness.
She learned that grace is no wage owed to merit, but the free gift of God she could only receive.

pos: noun (the putting to death of sin)
etymology: From the Latin mortificatio, a putting to death, from mors (death) and facere (to make); the Spirit-wrought slaying of indwelling sin in the believer.
biblical_def: Mortification is the believer's lifelong work, wrought by the Holy Spirit, of putting to death the deeds of the body and the remaining corruption of indwelling sin. The apostle commands it directly: “If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live,” and “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” It rests upon a finished fact—the old man is crucified with Christ, and they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts—and it issues in a continual duty: the believer must daily slay what Christ has already condemned. John Owen's famous maxim states the doctrine's urgency: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.” Mortification is not the eradication of sin in this life, for the flesh lusts against the Spirit to the end; nor is it mere outward restraint, the cutting off of acts while the root is cherished; it is the weakening, starving, and slaying of sin at its root by the power of the indwelling Spirit, through faith in Christ, by the means of grace. The dictionary marks the doctrine against two errors: the perfectionism that claims sin can be wholly rooted out now, and the therapeutic spirit that reframes sin as mere brokenness to be managed and healed rather than mortified. The believer does not negotiate with his sin or merely cope with it; by the Spirit he puts it to death, the negative side of that sanctification whose positive side is the quickening of the new man unto holiness.
webster_summary: The Spirit-wrought putting to death of indwelling sin in the believer (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5), resting on the old man's crucifixion with Christ; not eradication nor mere restraint, but the daily slaying of sin at the root.
webster_full: MORTIFICATION, noun. [Latin mors, death, and facere, to make.] The putting to death of indwelling sin by the Spirit.
“If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Romans 8:13).
It rests on a finished fact: the old man is crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6).
It is not eradication of sin in this life, nor mere outward restraint, but the slaying of sin at its root.
Owen: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”
scriptures: For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Ro 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
corruption_summary: Perfectionism claims sin can be wholly eradicated now, while the therapeutic spirit reframes sin as brokenness to be managed and healed rather than put to death.
corruption_paragraphs: Perfectionism, in its Wesleyan and Keswick and modern revivalist forms, teaches that the believer may reach a state in which indwelling sin is eradicated or rendered inactive, often by a single crisis of consecration. The dictionary rejects this. Scripture commands ongoing mortification precisely because sin remains: the flesh lusts against the Spirit to the end of life, and the apostle who said the old man was crucified still commanded daily slaying of its deeds. To claim sin gone is to deceive oneself; the duty of mortification is lifelong because the warfare is lifelong.

The more fashionable corruption is the therapeutic, which relabels sin as “brokenness,” “woundedness,” or “unhealthy patterns” to be managed, processed, and healed, rather than confessed and mortified. This empties the doctrine of its moral seriousness and its hope. Scripture does not call the believer to manage his lusts but to kill them, not to cope with sin but to crucify it, by the power of the indwelling Spirit. The dictionary recovers mortification as real spiritual warfare: sin is an enemy to be slain, not a condition to be soothed, and the Spirit gives the believer both the duty and the strength to put it to death.
roots_summary: From the Latin mors (death) and facere (to make); the Greek thanatoo (to put to death) and nekroo (to mortify) name the slaying of the deeds of the body.
roots_lines: Mors, Latin, death; mortificare, to put to death, the root of “mortify.”
Thanatoo, Greek, to put to death, in Romans 8:13.
Nekroo, Greek, to make dead or mortify, in Colossians 3:5.
Stauroo, Greek, to crucify, of the flesh crucified with its affections (Galatians 5:24).
The “old man” (Greek palaios anthropos) is the unregenerate self crucified with Christ.
usage: The pastor pressed Owen's maxim, that the believer must be killing sin daily or sin will be killing him.
He warned against the therapy that manages sin instead of mortifying it by the Spirit.
She set herself, in the strength of the indwelling Spirit, to starve and slay the lust she once cherished.

pos: noun phrase (acknowledgment of sin to God)
etymology: From the Latin confessio, an acknowledgment, from confiteri (to acknowledge fully); the believer's humble acknowledgment of sin before God, with a view to pardon and cleansing.
biblical_def: Confession of sin is the believer's honest and humble acknowledgment of his sin before God, owning it as sin, taking God's side against himself, and seeking pardon and cleansing through Christ. It is grounded in the gospel promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” The wisdom of Proverbs sets confession against concealment: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.” David traces the whole experience in the Psalms—the misery of unconfessed sin, when his bones waxed old through his roaring all the day long, and the relief of acknowledgment: “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid… and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” True confession is more than admitting facts; it is the broken and contrite heart that names sin honestly, hates it, and forsakes it. The dictionary distinguishes the biblical doctrine from the Roman sacrament of auricular confession, in which sins are confessed to a priest for absolution and assigned penance; Scripture directs confession to God through the one Mediator, with mutual confession among believers commended for healing and prayer, but never a priestly tribunal as the appointed channel of forgiveness. Nor is confession a mere therapeutic unburdening that eases the conscience without repentance. It is the godward acknowledgment of sin by a soul that trusts the faithful and just God to forgive for Christ's sake, the daily exercise of the justified sinner who still walks in a body of death.
webster_summary: The believer's humble, godward acknowledgment of sin, owning it and forsaking it, seeking pardon and cleansing through Christ (1 John 1:9); distinct from Roman auricular confession and from mere therapeutic unburdening.
webster_full: CONFESSION OF SIN, noun phrase. [Latin confessio, acknowledgment.] The humble owning of sin before God for pardon and cleansing.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us” (1 John 1:9).
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper; whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy (Proverbs 28:13).
It is the broken and contrite heart that names, hates, and forsakes sin.
Directed to God through Christ, not to a priest for sacramental absolution.
scriptures: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
corruption_summary: Rome channels confession through a priest's tribunal and penance, while the therapeutic age reduces it to an unburdening that eases the conscience without repentance or forsaking of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman sacrament of penance requires the confession of mortal sins to a priest, who pronounces absolution and assigns satisfaction, making the priesthood the appointed channel of forgiveness. The dictionary rejects this on the ground of the one Mediator: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the believer confesses his sin directly to God through Him. Scripture commends believers confessing their faults one to another for prayer and healing, but it knows no priestly tribunal whose absolution forgives sins; that prerogative belongs to God alone.

The fashionable corruption is therapeutic. Confession is recast as catharsis—an unburdening that relieves guilt feelings, validates the self, and asks no repentance. But biblical confession takes God's side against the sin, hates it, and forsakes it; the one who only covers his sin or merely vents it shall not prosper. The dictionary recovers confession as the godward acknowledgment of a broken and contrite heart that trusts the faithful and just God to forgive for Christ's sake—not a technique for feeling better, but the honest repentance of a soul that has seen its sin as God sees it.
roots_summary: From the Latin confiteri (to acknowledge fully) and the Greek homologeo (to say the same thing, to agree); to confess sin is to say the same of it that God says.
roots_lines: Homologeo, Greek, to confess, literally “to say the same thing,” to agree with God about sin.
Confiteri, Latin, to acknowledge or own fully, the root of “confession.”
Yadah, Hebrew, to confess or acknowledge, used in the penitential Psalms.
Nashbar / dakka, the “broken and contrite” heart of Psalm 51:17.
“Faithful and just” (1 John 1:9) grounds forgiveness in God's character and Christ's satisfaction.
usage: The pastor led the congregation in confession of sin, that they might take God's side against themselves.
He distinguished biblical confession to God from the Roman tribunal of the priest.
She found that covering her sin brought misery, but confessing and forsaking it brought mercy.

etymology: From “natural” (Latin naturalis) and “revelation” (Latin revelatio, an unveiling); God's disclosure of Himself through the created order and conscience, distinct from special revelation in Scripture.
biblical_def: Natural revelation, also called general revelation, is God's disclosure of Himself to all men through the works of creation, the ordering of providence, and the witness of conscience, as distinct from the special revelation given in His Word. The apostle declares it clearly: “The invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse.” The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth His handywork; day unto day uttereth speech. God left not Himself without witness, giving rain and fruitful seasons and filling men's hearts with food and gladness. The dictionary affirms that natural revelation truly makes God known—His existence, His eternal power and Godhead, His goodness, and the work of His law written on the conscience—so that it renders all men without excuse and is the ground of their just condemnation. Yet it also affirms, with the Reformed confessions, that natural revelation is not sufficient to save. It tells of God the Creator but not of God the Redeemer; it shows His power and wrath but not the gospel of Christ. Fallen men, moreover, suppress this knowledge in unrighteousness, exchanging the truth of God for idols. Therefore special revelation in Scripture is necessary, not to begin the knowledge of God but to give the saving knowledge of Him in Christ that nature can never supply.
webster_summary: God's disclosure of Himself through creation, providence, and conscience (Romans 1:20; Psalm 19:1), making His power and Godhead known to all and leaving them without excuse; true but insufficient to save, and suppressed by fallen men.
webster_full: NATURAL REVELATION, noun phrase. God's disclosure of Himself through the created order, providence, and conscience.
“The invisible things of him… are clearly seen… so that they are without excuse” (Romans 1:20).
The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1).
It reveals God the Creator, His power and goodness, but not God the Redeemer.
True but insufficient to save; suppressed by fallen men, who exchange the truth for idols.
scriptures: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge.
Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
corruption_summary: Natural theology overreaches when it claims nature can yield a saving knowledge of God, while atheistic naturalism denies that creation reveals God at all; both depart from the apostle's balance.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption, found in some forms of natural theology, overreaches the witness of creation, supposing that unaided reason can ascend from nature to a saving knowledge of God, or that natural revelation needs no correction or completion by Scripture. The dictionary, with the Reformed confessions, denies this. Natural revelation discloses the Creator's power and Godhead and binds the conscience, but it knows nothing of Christ, the cross, or the way of pardon. The saving knowledge of God comes only by special revelation; nature condemns but cannot redeem.

The opposite corruption is the atheistic naturalism of the age, which denies that the creation reveals God at all and explains the cosmos without a Creator. The apostle answers it: the invisible things of God are clearly seen in the things that are made, so that men are without excuse. Unbelief is not for want of evidence but a suppression of the truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18). The dictionary holds the apostle's balance: creation genuinely and inescapably reveals God, leaving every man accountable; and Scripture alone reveals the Saviour, so that the testimony of the stars must be completed by the testimony of the Word.
roots_summary: From the Latin revelatio (an unveiling) applied to natura (creation); the Reformed term “general revelation” marks its universal reach, against the “special revelation” of Scripture.
roots_lines: Revelatio, Latin, an unveiling or disclosure, the root of “revelation.”
“General” revelation: given to all men everywhere through creation and conscience.
“Special” revelation: God's saving self-disclosure in His Word and in Christ.
Anapologetos, Greek, “without excuse” (Romans 1:20), the effect of natural revelation.
The conscience and the “work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans 2:15) belong to it.
usage: The apologist argued from natural revelation that men are without excuse, yet pointed them to Scripture for the Saviour.
He warned against a natural theology that thinks nature can teach the gospel, which only the Word reveals.
She saw the glory of God in the heavens, and gave thanks for the Scripture that told her His name in Christ.

pos: noun phrase (an order instituted at creation)
etymology: From “creation” and “ordinance” (Latin ordinare, to set in order); the institutions God established at creation, before the fall, binding upon all mankind.
biblical_def: A creation ordinance is an order or institution established by God at the creation, before the fall, and therefore binding upon all mankind in every age, not merely upon the redeemed or upon Israel under the law. The Reformed tradition counts chiefly three. The first is marriage and the family: God made them male and female, and said, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh,” with the blessing to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The second is labour and dominion: the LORD God took the man and put him into the garden to dress it and to keep it, and gave mankind dominion over the works of His hands—work is not a curse but a creational good, though the fall brought toil and thorns. The third is the Sabbath: God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, resting from His work, setting a pattern of one day's rest in seven woven into the very fabric of the week. The dictionary holds that these ordinances, being grounded in creation and not in the Mosaic economy, abide for all peoples; they are not optional cultural arrangements but the architecture of human life as God designed it. This is the dictionary's answer to the spirit of the age that treats marriage, the two sexes, work, and rest as social constructs to be redefined at will. They were instituted by the Creator before sin entered, and what God ordained at the beginning man may not lawfully overturn.
webster_summary: An institution God established at creation before the fall, binding on all mankind—chiefly marriage and family, labour and dominion, and the Sabbath; the architecture of human life as designed, not social constructs to be redefined.
webster_full: CREATION ORDINANCE, noun phrase. An order instituted by God at creation, before the fall, binding upon all mankind.
Marriage and family: a man shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh (Genesis 2:24).
Labour and dominion: the man was put in the garden to dress and keep it (Genesis 2:15).
The Sabbath: God blessed and sanctified the seventh day, resting from His work (Genesis 2:3).
Grounded in creation, not the Mosaic law, these ordinances abide for every age and people.
scriptures: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Ge 2:3
And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.

And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: The spirit of the age treats marriage, the two sexes, work, and rest as social constructs to be redefined at will, denying that the Creator fixed these orders before the fall.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning ideology holds that marriage, sex, family, and even the rhythm of work and rest are social constructs—arrangements built by culture and therefore open to redefinition by culture. The dictionary names this as a corruption of the creation ordinances. God instituted marriage as one man and one woman, made mankind male and female, gave work and dominion, and sanctified the Sabbath rest, all before sin entered the world. These are not the customs of a tribe but the architecture of humanity as such, written into creation by the Creator's hand.

Because they are creational and not merely Mosaic, the ordinances bind all men, not only the church or ancient Israel. Hence the Sabbath principle of one day's rest in seven predates Sinai; hence marriage is honourable among all and its bond inviolable; hence honest labour is a creational good and idleness a disorder. The dictionary recovers the ordinances as God's good design for the whole human race, against both the legalism that would bind men to Mosaic ceremonies and the revolutionary spirit that would tear up the Creator's order itself. What God ordained at the beginning, no parliament or fashion may lawfully overturn.
roots_summary: From the Latin ordinare (to set in order); an “ordinance” is an appointed order, here one fixed at creation (creatio) and so prior to the fall and the law.
roots_lines: Ordinare, Latin, to set in order or appoint, the root of “ordinance.”
The ordinances are pre-fall: instituted in Eden before sin entered.
Marriage rests on “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), the foundation of the family.
Labour rests on “dress it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), work as creational good.
The Sabbath rests on God's own resting and sanctifying of the seventh day (Genesis 2:3).
usage: The pastor taught that marriage is a creation ordinance, fixed before the fall, and no construct of culture.
He grounded the Sabbath principle in creation, predating Sinai and binding upon all.
She honoured honest labour as a creational good, given before the curse turned it to toil.

etymology: From the Greek katecheo, to sound down, to instruct by word of mouth; the systematic instruction of believers and their children in the doctrines of the faith, often by question and answer.
biblical_def: Catechesis is the ordered instruction of believers, and especially of children and new converts, in the doctrines of the Christian faith, that they may know what they believe and why. The word comes from the Greek katecheo, to teach by word of mouth, used by Paul when he says, “Let him that is taught (katechoumenos) in the word communicate unto him that teacheth.” Its roots run deep into the covenant: God charged Israel to teach His words diligently unto their children, talking of them in the house and by the way, when they lie down and when they rise up; fathers are to bring their children up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord; and Timothy from a child had known the holy scriptures which are able to make wise unto salvation. The Reformation recovered catechesis as a chief instrument of reform, producing the great catechisms—Luther's Small Catechism, the Heidelberg, the Westminster Shorter and Larger, and the Baptist Catechism—in which the faith is set out by question and answer, to be learned, recited, and understood. The dictionary commends catechesis as a duty of parents and the church against two modern neglects: the entertainment-driven children's ministry that amuses without instructing, leaving a generation ignorant of doctrine; and the anti-creedal sentiment that despises formal teaching as “head knowledge” opposed to a living faith. True faith has content; it must be known to be believed and confessed. Catechesis is the patient handing-down of that content from one generation to the next, that children of the covenant may grow up grounded in the truth and ready to give an answer for the hope within them.
webster_summary: The ordered instruction of believers and their children in the doctrines of the faith, often by question and answer (Greek katecheo, to teach by word of mouth); a covenant duty recovered by the Reformation, against entertainment-driven and anti-creedal neglect.
webster_full: CATECHESIS, noun. [Greek katecheo, to sound down, to instruct orally.] Ordered instruction in the doctrines of the faith.
“Let him that is taught (katechoumenos) in the word communicate unto him that teacheth” (Galatians 6:6).
Rooted in the command to teach God's words diligently to children (Deuteronomy 6:7).
Recovered by the Reformation in the great catechisms, taught by question and answer.
A duty of parents and the church, that the faith may be known, believed, and confessed.
scriptures: De 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Ga 6:6
Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.
corruption_summary: The entertainment-driven children's ministry amuses without instructing, and the anti-creedal spirit despises doctrinal teaching as mere “head knowledge,” leaving a generation ignorant of the faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of doctrinal instruction. Much modern children's and youth ministry has traded catechesis for entertainment, substituting games, music, and emotional experience for the patient teaching of doctrine, so that young people are amused for years and emerge unable to state what they believe or why. The dictionary names this a grievous neglect of the covenant charge to teach God's words diligently to the next generation. A faith never taught is a faith easily abandoned.

A subtler corruption is the anti-creedal sentiment that pits a “living relationship” against “head knowledge,” despising catechisms and formal doctrine as cold and lifeless. But Scripture knows no faith without content: it must be known to be believed, and confessed to be held. The great catechisms exist precisely to serve a living faith by grounding it in truth. The dictionary recovers catechesis as the church's and the home's appointed means of handing down the faith—not the enemy of heartfelt religion but its necessary foundation, that children of the covenant may be made wise unto salvation through the knowledge of the holy scriptures.
roots_summary: From the Greek katecheo (to sound down into the ears, to instruct orally); whence “catechism” (the book of instruction) and “catechumen” (one being instructed).
roots_lines: Katecheo, Greek, to teach by word of mouth, to instruct, “to sound down.”
Katechoumenos, Greek, “one who is taught,” whence “catechumen.”
“Catechism,” the ordered book of question and answer for instruction.
The covenant root: “teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deuteronomy 6:7).
The “nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4) is the fatherly duty of instruction.
usage: The elders restored catechesis, teaching the children the Shorter Catechism by question and answer.
He warned that a ministry which only amuses leaves a generation unable to confess the faith.
She catechized her little ones at the table, talking of God's words when they sat in the house.

etymology: From the Authorized Version of the Sermon on the Mount; the enduring riches the disciple is to lay up with God, against the perishing treasures of earth.
biblical_def: Treasures in heaven are the enduring riches that the disciple of Christ is commanded to lay up with God, in contrast to the perishing treasures of earth. In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord commands, “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven… For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” The teaching is not that wealth is sin, nor that the believer earns heaven by giving, but that he is to invest his life and substance in what cannot perish, securing for himself a treasure in the heavens that faileth not. These heavenly treasures include the eternal inheritance kept for the saints, the reward of grace for faithful service, and the fruit of generosity, of suffering for Christ, and of souls won. The Lord grounds the command in a law of the heart: a man's treasure draws his affections, so that he who heaps earthly riches binds his heart to a dying world, while he who lays up treasure in heaven sets his affection on things above. The dictionary holds the doctrine against two errors. The prosperity gospel inverts the Lord's words, promising earthly treasure as the reward of faith and binding the heart to the very mammon Christ warned against. The opposite error, a false asceticism, despises all earthly goods as evil rather than using them as stewardship toward heaven. The believer is to hold the things of earth loosely and lay up what endures, that his heart may be where his true and lasting riches are.
webster_summary: The enduring riches the disciple lays up with God (Matthew 6:20), against the perishing treasures of earth; for where the treasure is, the heart follows—the rebuke of the prosperity gospel and of mammon-bound affections alike.
webster_full: TREASURES IN HEAVEN, noun phrase. The enduring riches the disciple lays up with God, beyond the reach of moth, rust, and thief.
“Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven… For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:20-21).
Against earthly treasures, where moth and rust corrupt and thieves steal (Matthew 6:19).
A treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth (Luke 12:33).
Not earning heaven, but investing the life and substance in what cannot perish.
scriptures: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel inverts the Lord's words, promising earthly treasure as faith's reward, while a false asceticism despises earthly goods rather than stewarding them toward heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel directly contradicts the Lord's command, promising believers earthly treasure—wealth, health, prosperity—as the reward of faith and giving. This binds the heart to the very mammon Christ told His disciples not to lay up, and makes the gospel a means to the riches that moth and rust corrupt. The dictionary names it a corruption: the Lord commanded treasure laid up in heaven, not on earth, and warned that no man can serve God and mammon. The preacher who promises earthly gain in exchange for faith preaches the opposite of the Sermon on the Mount.

The opposite corruption is a false asceticism that treats all earthly goods as evil, despising property, comfort, and provision as though poverty were itself holiness. But the Lord does not forbid the use of earthly things; He forbids the hoarding of them as treasure and the binding of the heart to them. The believer is a steward who holds the goods of earth loosely and lays up what endures—by generosity, by faithful service, by suffering for Christ, by winning souls. The dictionary recovers the doctrine: earthly things are to be used for heavenly ends, and the heart set where the true treasure is, with God.
roots_summary: From the Greek thesauros (a treasure, store, or treasury), whence “thesaurus”; the heavenly treasure is laid up (thesaurizo) where no corruption can reach it.
roots_lines: Thesauros, Greek, a treasure or storehouse, the word in Matthew 6:20.
Thesaurizo, Greek, to lay up or store treasure.
“Moth” (ses) and “rust” (brosis, eating away) figure the decay of earthly goods.
“Mammon” (Aramaic, riches personified) is the rival master Christ names.
“Where your treasure is” sets the law of the heart following its treasure.
usage: The pastor preached treasures in heaven to rebuke the prosperity gospel that binds the heart to earthly gain.
He held his property loosely, laying up what endures by generosity and faithful service.
She set her affection on things above, knowing her heart would follow her treasure.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Hebrew bene ha-Elohim and the Greek huioi tou Theou; a title used in Scripture of angels, and supremely of believers adopted in Christ.
biblical_def: “Sons of God” is a biblical title used in more than one sense, whose crown and fulness is the adoption of believers into the family of God through Jesus Christ. In its highest covenant use it names the redeemed: “As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name”; “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God”; “Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God.” This sonship is not by nature but by grace and adoption, for the only-begotten Son is alone the Son by eternal generation; believers are made sons by union with Him, receiving the Spirit of adoption whereby they cry, Abba, Father. The dictionary notes the term's other uses without confusing them: in Job and elsewhere the “sons of God” are the angels, the heavenly host that stand before the LORD; and the disputed “sons of God” of Genesis 6 have been understood variously—most soberly, in the Reformed tradition, as the godly line of Seth intermarrying with the ungodly line of Cain, though some read them as fallen angels or as dynastic rulers. The dictionary does not bind the conscience on Genesis 6 but holds the saving sense as the heart of the title: in Christ, by adoption, sinners become the sons of God, heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ, awaiting the manifestation of the sons of God when creation itself shall be delivered into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
webster_summary: A biblical title used of angels (Job 1:6) and supremely of believers adopted in Christ (John 1:12; Romans 8:14); the saving sense—sonship by grace and adoption, not nature—is its crown, with the disputed Genesis 6 usage left unbound.
webster_full: SONS OF GOD, noun phrase. [Hebrew bene ha-Elohim; Greek huioi tou Theou.] A title used of angels and of adopted believers.
Of believers: to as many as received Him He gave power to become the sons of God (John 1:12).
As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God (Romans 8:14).
This sonship is by grace and adoption, not by nature, through union with the only-begotten Son.
Of angels in Job; the disputed Genesis 6 usage is left unbound, the Sethite reading the soberest.
scriptures: Joh 1:12
But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.
Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God: therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not.
Ga 4:6
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
corruption_summary: Liberal theology dissolves the title into a universal “fatherhood of God and brotherhood of man,” making all men sons by nature and denying the sonship that comes only by adoption in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The great liberal corruption of this title is the doctrine of the universal “fatherhood of God and brotherhood of man,” which holds that all human beings are by nature the children of God, needing no new birth or adoption. The dictionary rejects this on the plain teaching of Scripture. By nature men are children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3); only those who receive Christ are given power to become the sons of God. God is the Father of all as Creator, but the saving sonship—the adoption into His family, the right to cry Abba, Father, the inheritance with Christ—belongs only to those united to the Son by faith.

A second confusion arises from the various uses of the phrase. Because “sons of God” names angels in Job and figures in the contested account of Genesis 6, some build elaborate and speculative doctrines, especially of angelic intermarriage with men. The dictionary counsels sobriety: the Reformed tradition has most often read the Genesis 6 “sons of God” as the godly Sethite line, and the conscience is not bound on the question. What is certain and central is the gospel sense—that sinners become the sons of God by grace, through adoption, in Jesus Christ, awaiting the glorious liberty of the children of God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew bene ha-Elohim (sons of God) and the Greek huioi / tekna tou Theou (sons / children of God); the title of adoption rests on union with the only-begotten Son.
roots_lines: Bene ha-Elohim, Hebrew, “sons of God,” used of the angelic host in Job 1:6.
Huioi tou Theou, Greek, “sons of God,” of believers led by the Spirit (Romans 8:14).
Tekna Theou, Greek, “children of God,” the term of John's Gospel and epistle.
Huiothesia, Greek, “adoption as sons,” the grace by which sinners become sons.
“Abba, Father” (Galatians 4:6) is the cry of the Spirit of adoption.
usage: The pastor preached that men are sons of God not by nature but by adoption in Christ, against the liberal gospel.
He counselled sobriety on the “sons of God” of Genesis 6, the Sethite reading being the soundest.
She marvelled at the manner of love that she, a sinner, should be called a child of God.

etymology: From “marriage” (Old French mariage) and “covenant” (Latin convenire, to come together in agreement); the lifelong covenant bond of one man and one woman before God.
biblical_def: The marriage covenant is the solemn, lifelong bond of one man and one woman, made before God, by which they become one flesh. Scripture names marriage not a mere contract of convenience but a covenant: the LORD is witness between a man and the wife of his youth, who is his companion and the wife of his covenant; the adulteress forsakes the guide of her youth and forgetteth the covenant of her God. The bond was instituted at creation, before the fall, when God made them male and female and said a man should leave his father and mother and cleave unto his wife, and they two should be one flesh—words the Lord Jesus reaffirmed, adding, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” The apostle lifts marriage to its highest meaning, declaring it a figure of Christ and the church: as the husband is head of the wife, so Christ is head of the church; and the one-flesh union is a great mystery concerning Christ and His people. The dictionary holds the marriage covenant against the corruptions of the age: the no-fault divorce that treats the bond as dissoluble at will, the cohabitation that takes the union without the covenant, and the redefinition of marriage to include what God never joined. Marriage is covenantal—binding, exclusive, and lifelong—ordered in the complementary headship and submission of husband and wife, and it images the unbreakable covenant love of Christ for His bride. To keep it is to honour the God who instituted it; to break it is to deal treacherously against the wife or husband of one's covenant and against the LORD who witnessed the vow.
webster_summary: The solemn, lifelong covenant bond of one man and one woman before God, instituted at creation and reaffirmed by Christ (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:6); a figure of Christ and the church, against no-fault divorce, cohabitation, and redefinition.
webster_full: MARRIAGE COVENANT, noun phrase. The lifelong covenant of one man and one woman before God, by which they become one flesh.
Scripture calls the wife “the wife of thy covenant” (Malachi 2:14), with the LORD as witness.
Instituted at creation: a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife (Genesis 2:24).
Reaffirmed by Christ: what God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matthew 19:6).
A figure of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32); binding, exclusive, and lifelong.
scriptures: Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Eph 5:31
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.
Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God.
corruption_summary: No-fault divorce treats the bond as dissoluble at will, cohabitation takes the union without the covenant, and the redefinition of marriage joins what God never joined.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern age has assaulted the marriage covenant from several sides. No-fault divorce treats the lifelong bond as a contract dissoluble at the will of either party, against the Lord's word that man may not put asunder what God has joined; widespread cohabitation takes the one-flesh union while refusing the covenant that sanctifies it; and the legal redefinition of marriage purports to join what God never joined, severing the institution from the male-and-female creation order on which it rests. The dictionary names these as corruptions of a creation ordinance, not mere shifts in social custom.

The recovery is the covenantal and christological nature of marriage. It is a covenant, with the LORD as witness, and therefore binding, exclusive, and lifelong; the spouse who breaks it deals treacherously against the partner and against God. And it is a figure of the gospel: the husband's headship images Christ's love for the church, the wife's submission images the church's response, and the unbreakable bond images the covenant faithfulness of Christ to His bride. The dictionary holds, with Scripture, that to honour the marriage covenant is to honour the God who instituted it and the gospel it was made to display.
roots_summary: From the Latin convenire (to come together, agree), the root of “covenant”; the Hebrew berith (covenant) names marriage a sworn bond, not a mere contract.
roots_lines: Berith, Hebrew, a covenant or sworn bond, applied to marriage in Malachi 2:14.
Convenire, Latin, to come together in agreement, the root of “covenant.”
“One flesh” (Hebrew basar echad) names the creational union of Genesis 2:24.
Mysterion, Greek, the “great mystery” of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32).
“The wife of thy youth” marks the covenant's lifelong intent.
usage: The pastor preached marriage as a covenant with the LORD as witness, not a contract dissoluble at will.
He showed the one-flesh union to be a figure of Christ and the church, against every redefinition.
She honoured the covenant of her youth, knowing the LORD had witnessed the vow.
